questions.question_text:
Bananas are priced at $\$5.50$/kg.
What does this mean?

options.why: This reads the rate upside down; the slash means dollars for each kilogram.

options.text: Bananas cost $\$5.50$ however many kilograms are bought.
options.why: A rate gives a price for each kilogram, not one fixed total price.

options.text: Each kilogram costs $\$5.50$ more than the one before.
options.why: The rate gives the cost of every kilogram, not an increase from one kilogram to the next.

questions.solution_text:
The slash means 'for each'.
$\$5.50$/kg reads '$\$5.50$ for each kilogram'.

questions.question_text: Which units are most likely for the cost of building a new home?

options.why: Dollars per hour measures a wage; a building cost is quoted for each square metre of floor area.
People per day measures something like population growth, not a cost.
Kilometres per hour measures a speed, not a cost.

questions.solution_text:
A building cost compares money with the floor area built.
Money over area gives units of $\$$/m$^2$.

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: Ratios compare two similar quantities, while rates compare two quantities with __________ units.

options.why: This uses the unit relationship for a ratio instead of a rate.
This omits the units that a rate must specify.

options.text: Always kilometres and hours as their
options.why: This treats the units of speed as the units of every rate; rates can compare other quantities.

questions.solution_text:
Different.
Ratios compare two similar quantities, while rates compare two quantities with different units.
